headline: 30TB enterprise SSDs hit $22,600, costing 18.6x more than HDDs; supply sold out through 2027
summary: A 30TB TLC enterprise SSD now costs $22,600, a 6.5x increase from last year. Meanwhile, nearline HDD output from major vendors is sold out through 2027, driving up spot prices.
details: A 30TB TLC enterprise SSD now costs $22,600, an 18.6 times higher price per terabyte than an equivalent hard drive. This represents a 6.5x increase from the $3,460 price point just last year. These figures come from VDURA's August Flash Volatility Index.

The rising flash prices, which saw a further 5% increase in July, are making all-flash AI storage builds significantly more expensive. A 25PB all-flash system could cost $51.60 million, compared to $12.86 million for a hybrid SSD-plus-HDD system.

However, the hybrid option faces a major hurdle: hard drive availability. Seagate and Western Digital have informed investors that their nearline HDD output is completely sold out through 2027. This forces those without long-term contracts to pay significantly higher spot prices.

NAND contract prices are continuing to rise, with TrendForce reporting a 10-15% increase quarter-on-quarter for Q3, following 70-75% in Q2 and 55-60% in Q1. VDURA's Senior VP of Marketing, Erik Salo, suggests that "elevated flash pricing is structural."

VDURA's own index has shown significant shifts, revising its Q1 2026 TLC forecast from $10,950 in January to $17,500. Additionally, the 30TB HDD price has surged from $495 in Q3 2025 to $1,216 currently, a 2.5 times increase.

Both Western Digital and Seagate CEOs have confirmed their companies are sold out of nearline capacity for years. WD's CEO stated they are sold out for 2026, with agreements extending into 2027 and 2028. Seagate's CEO noted nearline capacity is almost fully allocated through calendar 2027 under build-to-order contracts.

Analysts estimate the HDD spot premium at 30% to 40%. For a "neocloud" without hyperscaler-scale supply agreements, acquiring these drives at spot prices, if at all possible, will push the cost of hybrid systems even higher than current estimates.

headline_marked: [[Ground LLM Answers in Live Coverage]] with a News Feed to improve AI output
headline: Ground LLM Answers in Live Coverage with a News Feed to improve AI output
summary: AI models often invent facts or provide stale information due to outdated training data. A structured, filterable news feed can ground LLM responses in current, verifiable facts.
details: Chatbots and research agents frequently invent partnerships, mix up CEOs, or cite non-existent sources when asked about current events. This happens because model weights are stale and generic web scrapes are noisy, leading to confident but fictional outputs.

The solution to this problem is a dedicated news feed for AI. This feed provides structured, filterable coverage that can be retrieved first and then passed into the LLM prompt as evidence, ensuring answers are based on published facts.

Without retrieval, LLMs rely on training cutoffs and pattern completion, failing when live news is required. This leads to stale knowledge, homonym collisions (e.g., 'Stripe' vs. unrelated 'Stripe' references), lack of citations, and unscoped volume from the open web.

A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) news feed keeps the model honest by using a filtered news data corpus instead of the entire internet. This involves treating an articles API as the retrieval layer for LLM context news.

For implementation, developers can use APIs like Perigon Articles (/v1/all), filtering by companyId, sorting by date, and limiting the size to 5-15 articles. This ensures the context pack is relevant and manageable for the model.

To prevent homonym collisions, specific entity IDs like personWikidataId can be used for targeted searches, ensuring accuracy when querying about individuals like Patrick Collison, rather than generic name matches.

The Stories API (/v1/stories/all) can be used for narrative clusters, compressing multiple near-duplicate headlines about a single event (e.g., a partnership announcement) into a more prompt-efficient format.

Retrieval alone is insufficient; grounding LLM quality also depends on careful instruction and size discipline. It's crucial to instruct the model to admit gaps when the context pack is empty and to prioritize recent, entity-pinned hits over large, unsorted data dumps.

Further quality can be achieved by using sourceGroup filters (e.g., top100) and excluding labels like Opinion, Paid News, or Press Release to ensure only third-party reporting is used. Each API hit provides essential fields like title, URL, publication date, publisher, and summary.
